A Desperado's End—Riddled With Bullets from an Officers' Posse.

CHICAGO, Dec. 3. The usual Sunday quiet in this city was rudely disturbed this afternoon by the report of the tragic arrest and shooting of the notorious Bill Allen, the Republican deserado, who murdered Officer Clarence E. Wright on last Wednesday night while resisting his arrest and made his escape. The entire police force of the city has been searching for the murderer ever since and several arrests were made in this and neighboring cities, but Allen succeeded in concealing himself until this afternoon, when he went to the house of a friend in the heart of the city and demanded food. A little girl recognized him and informed the police, who surrounded the house. Allen finding himself in a trap fought like a wild beast at bay, emptying his revolvers on the officers and dangerously wounding Policeman Melville in the back. Police officer returned the fire and Allen was riddled with bullets receiving six mortal wounds. The news of his death caused much excitement.

The news of the tragic death of the negro who has braved the entire police force of the city for months past spread like wildfire. ALLEGED MURDERER ACQUITTED.
[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

Fergus Falls, Dec. 3.—The jury in the Christie murder case were charged by the judge after Erwin's closing speech at 11 o'clock last night. The jury were out all night. At 9 o'clock this morning an agreement was announced. The court officers, judge, jury and Christie were summoned and a verdict rendered of not guilty. Great congratulations to the prisoner followed.

The Fergus Falls Daily Telegram, at the commencement of the case gave the following statement:

This case was on the calendar last spring but was continued to the present term. The facts are very peculiar. Stull, the murdered man, and Christie, the defendant, were old friends. On the afternoon of March 29, Stull started from Bluffton to go to New York Mills. Christie, who was preparing to follow his wife and infant child to Iowa, where they had gone but a few days before, accompanied Stull on the road a distance of about four miles to a place where Christie was to remain all night. The next morning the body of Stull was found about a mile from where Christie was to have parted from him. As they were seen together the night before, suspicion pointed to Christie, who, the next morning, had started on his way to Iowa. Christie had proceeded leisurely about forty miles when he was arrested at Spruce Hill, Douglas county, and brought back to Bluffton, where a great crowd had gathered. Threats of lynching were indulged in freely and at this time and under these circumstances Christie made a confession of guilt, the truth of which he now denies, but which the prosecution will probably try to use against him. Immediately following the event last spring, considerable feeling was manifested against the defendant, as frequently happens in such cases. The people have, since then, had time for reflection, and public opinion can fairly be said to have changed considerably in his favor.

THE MURDEROUS BILL ALLEN KILLED.

[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

Chicago, Dec. 3.—Bill Allen, a negro desperado, made a murderous assault on a comrade last week and when the police tried to arrest him, he shot Officer Wright dead. This afternoon he was discovered secreted in the rear of a residence, 134 North Halstead street, and the police again made an attack, when Allen shot Officer Mulenhill through the hand, the ball also striking near the eye, causing a serious wound. An alarm was turned on and officers hastened to the scene from all stations. Allen was discovered in a large dry goods box, and in attempting to escape was shot four times by Sergeant Wheeler and killed.

Officers Fletcher and Foley who were with Wright at the time he was killed, were to-day discharged by the chief of police for cowardice.

It seems after Allen escaped this afternoon from Officer Mulenhill, he fled west. A telegraph operator witnessing the battle turned in an alarm and patrol wagons quickly brought policemen from all stations, a formidable force. This, with a hundred citizens continued the search for the murderous fugitive, and at length found him secreted in a big dry goods box as stated. When the cover was raised the desperado leaped forth, poured a volley into the crowd, and ran but was brought to bay in a shed on West Kinzie street. Sergeant Wheeler opened upon him with a pistol in each hand, firing through a window, and succeeded in plumping four bullets into him. The villian, with a yell of rage, fell dead.

The procession of wagons, policemen, and citizens escorted the remains to the police station, where the body was exhibited in the window, thousands of people viewing the ghastly sight. It was like a day at the circus.

FOUL MURDER.
Officer Clarence E. Wright, of Chicago, Shot to Death While at His Post of Duty.
Officer Clarence E. Wright, of the Desplaines Street Station, Chicago, Ill., was foully murdered at 6:45 o'clock Saturday evening by a colored desperado named Bill Allen, familiarly known as the "Colonel," whom he was attempting to arrest. The scene of the murder was in one of the tumble-down rookeries on West Washington street, near Canal street, used as a lodging-house and tenement by low colored and disreputable white people. Officers Wright and T. Folev had been detailed by Captian Ronfield to assist Detective John Fletcher, the colored "fly" at Central Station, in arresting Allen, whose desperate character was only too well known by the officers. They were trying to get in his room at No. 37 West Washington street, and while Allen's woman, known as Aunie Hutchinson, was insisting that Allen was not there, the later suddenly threw the door wide open and fired directly at Wright, who staggered back and fell dead, with two bullets in the head. The other officers immediately drew their revolvers, and a number of shots were sent after Allen as he went down the stairs on the jump and escaped. An attempt was made to follow him, but without success. The body of

THE MURDERED OFFICER

was removed to the Desplaines street station, and on examination it was found that one bullet had entered the right temple and the other just under the outer corner of the right eye. The bullets had both lodged in the brain and death was almost instantaneous.

This was the second murderous affray in which Allen had participated during the day, and the murder of Officer Wright resulted from the attempt to arrest Allen for the first affair. Allen and another colored man named James Smead, who had been employed on Pullman palace cars on the Chicago & Northwestern railroad were discharged on the charge of stealing butter and provisions from the Pullman company. Allen was employed as a waiter and Smead as a cook. In the same working gang with them was William Jones, a colored waiter, whom the other two suspected of being the cause of their discharge. In fact, they had but little doubt, and while Jones was at work in one of the Pullman cars at the Chicago & Northwestern depot, corner Wells and Kinzie streets, they made a murderous assault upon him. Allen had a carpenter's hammer in his hand, and he thrice struck Jones viciously with it on the head, knocking him senseless.

LEAVING HIM FOR DEAD,
with a fractured skull. The murderous pair then ran out of the car and escaped. Jones was laid out on one of the berths, and Dr. Isham, the company physician, was immediately summoned. In dressing Jones' injuries he took ten splinters from the wounds. The Larrabee street patrol removed the injured man to the County Hospital, where the physicians in attendance examined the wounds and pronounced them exceedingly dangerous, probably fatal. Steps were immediately taken for the arrest of Allen and Smead, and the warrants intrusted to Detective John Fletcher. Not knowing Allen personally, though he had heard of his recklessness, he secured the assistance of William Hizer, of No. 174 Harrison street, who knew Allen, to point him out. They proceeded to the locality where Allen lived, and, after a short watch, were rewarded by seeing Allen enter the house. They saw him enter room 11, No. 37 West Washington street, and knew they had their man caged. Leaving Hizer to watch, the detective then made application to Captain Bonfield for assistance, feeling that Allen would not be easily taked and would

MAKE A DESPERATE FIGHT.

Officers Wright and Foley were sent, and returning to Hizer, they learned that Allen was still in the house. Leaving Foley down stairs, Fletcher, Wright and Hizer went up stairs. Wright rapped at the door, the other two standing slightly to one side. The Hutchinson woman opened the door, and in response to the officers inquiry for Allen, said he was not at home. Hizer, who knew different, insisted that he was in the room, and as the officers made an attempt to force open the door, it being then but slightly open, it was suddenly thrown back, exposing Allen with a cocked revolver. He commenced firing immediately, the first two bullets hitting Wright in the head. As he staggered back he interfered with Fletcher, Hizer being unarmed sprang back as Allen continued firing and gave him a free path down stairs. Fletcher emptied his revolver after Allen but, as far as known, without effect. On reaching the sidewalk

ALLEN TURNED AND FIRED

directly at Hizer, who was following, but did not hit him. He then ran north through the alley between Clinton and Canal streets, and it is believed afterward got to the South through the Washington street tunnel. The police are making strenuous efforts to capture him, but up to midnight had been unsuccessful. As he has many friends on the various Pullman cars running out of the city, the police fear that he might have got out on one, and have telegraphed a full description of him to the neighboring cities.

The murdered officer was a fine-looking man, about 28 years old, and the picture of physical health, and though but six months on the force, had done some excellent work and gave promise of being numbered among the best men of the force. He was the son of A. L. Wright, and lived with his parents and brothers and sisters, of whom he had eight, at No. 3835 Indiana avenue.

ANOTHER OF BILL ALLEN'S VICTIMS.

[Special Telegram to the Globe.]

CHICAGO, Dec. 11.—At the time of the shooting of Officer Patrick Mulvahill by the desperado, Bill Allen, the physicans in the case found half of the ball imbedded in the cavity over the left eye, and it was supposed they had removed all that had entered the wound. In view of this theory, it was announced that the wound was not dangerous and that the officer would soon be able to go on duty again. These hopes, however, have been dispelled by the condition of Officer Mulvahill during the last two or three days. Instead of healing the wound has continued to swell and grow worse and the wounded man has suffered intense paid. Yesterday Drs. Lee and Tenger performed a second operation, and made the startling discovery that the skull was fractured. Two pieces of the splintered ball were found immediately back of the eye bail, and two pieces of bone were extracted at the same time. A ROTTEN DETECTIVE FORCE.

WASHINGTON, Dec. 11.—The citizens' committee had an interview in jail to-day with O'Leary and Murphy, convicted three card monte men. Each detailed the circumstances of many robberies, including the government printing office money theft; gave the names of the thieves and
constances of many robberies, including the government printing office money theft; gave the names of the thieves and the detectives who "stood in" as well as the percentage of the proceeds of the robberies. They paid the detectives 20 per cent. Detectives, it was even said, planned the same jobs and selected the men to execute them. Murphy and O'Leary gave a circumstantial account of the Christiancy diamond robbery, and the alleged diamonds of the ex-minister, valued at from $15,000 to $20,000 were disposed of at a great sacrifice in New York, and a heavy percentage given to two detectives who are named. "The wife of one of the men," O'Leary said, "new wears dresses made from the silk taken in the Burdette robbery and given to the detective as his part of the pludder." It is alleged the entire detective force of the district receives dividends levied weekly on bunko and monte men. The detectives involved, save one, who were dismissed for betraying the government's interests in the star route cases, are yet on the force. Magruder, a member of the committee, thought he recognized O'Leary, who is well educated, and asked him if he had ever been at college, O'Leary answered at Gonzuga college. "Then," said Magruder, "We were college mates. I now remember you well." O'Leary seemed greatly mortified at this identification.

WAXAHACHIE, Dec. 18.—[Speciul.]—The usual quiet of Waxahachie was plunged into a high state of excitement about 7 o'clock last evening. City Marshal J. H. Spalding, while attempting to arrest Charles Smith, a drunken and disorderly negro, was shot and instantly killed by Smith. The pistol was a forty-five calibre Bull-dog. The ball struck Mr. Spalding just above the left eye. T. K. Allen, deputy marshal, first attempted to arrest the negro, who resisted arrest at first, then ran, Allen firing at him several times, the negro returning the fire. Marshal Spalding, attracted by the firing, obtained a horse and went in pursuit, and after he had fired on him several times overtook him, dismounted and in attempting to make the arrest was killed. The news of the murder spread with lightning rapidity, and in a few minutes the town was thronged with armed men, and the clatter of horses' hoofs resounded on every avenue leading from town, all in pursuit of the murderer. Many went on foot in search, scouring every nook and corner, where it was thought he would hide, and a guard was placed to watch his house. About an hour after the killing the negro approached his house, the guard ordered him to throw up his hands and surrender. The response was two shots, fired at the guard, attended with curses and an order to get out of his way. The guard returned the fire and ran behind the house. [Special to the News and Courter.]

LANCASTER, August 9.—Hearing that a negro had been lynched last night near this place, your correspondent at an early hour this morning repaired to the scene, which is in a lonely spot about one and a half miles east of here. Arriving on the ground I found the body of a negro hanging from the limb of a small white oak tree with his toes touching terra firma. I gathered the following particulars: On Monday night, the 7th instant, Dan Blakeney, colored, who was employed as a farm hand by a prominent citizen of this county who lives fourteen miles east of this place, entered the room of the twelve-year old daughter of his employer and attempted to assault her. The screams of the child aroused the household and the villain fled without having accomplished his hellish purpose. He was pursued and captured and confessed everything. A posse of constables started to jail with the fiend, but when about two miles from Lancaster an engaged body of good citizens took fercible possession of Dan Blakeney and hung him to a convenient tree. That he met a just but terrible fate is the verdict of all, both white and colored.

Yesterday another negro was lodged in our county jail for committing a rape on a mulatto girl. Serious threats of lynching are being made by the colored people.

E. B. R.

In the northern part of the State the Republican-Independent-Greenback State ticket was successful in many counties. Calbert, Shulman, DeKalb, Elmore, Erowah, Laurence, Lauderdale, Limestone, Jackson, Madison and Morgan have elected Independents to the Legislature. In a number of counties the Democrats have been successful by only narrow majorities and in others the official count will be necessary to decide the result. THE KEMPER HORROR.
The Outrage On, and Murder of, Mrs.
Callie Henson.
*THE BRUTE LYNCHED.
We have some further particulars of the late horrible crime in Kemper county and the subsequent lynching of the murderer, obtained from parties who reside in the vicinity of the occurrence. Mr. Aleck Henson was married last December to Miss Callie Echols, who was but 17 years of age and the daughter of Osborne Echols, a substantial farmer of Neshoba county. After marriage he settled on a farm in Kemper county, near the Neshoba line. On Thursday morning he left home early, taking his dinner with him, to plough on his farm, about a mile and a half from his residence. He returned late, and could see nothing of his wife. He called her but with no response, and finally, supposing she had gone to a neighbor's, started to look for her. A negro named George Hughes, who was a tenant on Henson's farm, and lived with his family in a cabin a few hundred yards from the house, came up to assist in the search, and as Henson was going off, told him to look in the well, that she might be there. The negro took a pole, put it in the well and cried out he had found her body. The well was eight or ten feet deep and full of water. Assistance was obtained and the dead body of Mrs. Henson was taken from the well. It was seen from examination of the body that she was first murdered and then thrown in the well. Her hair was dishevelled and there were marks of violence on her throat—the imprint of fingers by which she had been strangled. The right ear was bitten nearly off, and the impression made by four human teeth was clearly seen. An inquest was held on the body Friday morning before Isaac Dawes, Justice of the Peace, and after hearing all the testimony, there was no doubt that she came to her death from violence. Suspicion was directed towards the negro Hughes and he was arrested. The fact that he suggested she might have fallen into the well, his presence on the place after Mr. Henson left, the marks of violence, and many other circumstances pointed to his guilt. Among them was the fact that he had changed his clothes on Thursday, and when an effort was made to examine them it appears they had been washed by his wife. He had an examination before Esquire Dawes, which was not concluded until late Friday evening. He was ordered to be committed to jail, and Constable William Smith started with him to DeKalb, intending to take him there that night. About half a mile from where the trial was held, a crowd of about 75 persons took the prisoner from the officer and he was at once hung.

KEMPER TO THE FRONT AGAIN. Hell Broke Loose There. ANOTHER KEMPER TRAGEDY.
A diabolical deed was done in Western Kemper county on Thursday morning. Heck Hinson, a young man in the Terry settlement, had been married about last Christmas to a beautiful young wife, and they were living happily together until last Thursday morning. On that day he left his home to be gone all day. He never saw his wife alive again. Returning late, he missed her and was greatly troubled. He was about to go in search of her, when a negro man, a tenant, having his cabin near his residence, hinted that she might be in the well. The horrible suspicion aroused by the hint proved to be a terrible reality. The indications were that the negro had ravished her very soon after her husband had left her there alone to the tender mercies of a black demon. The breakfast table was standing as he left it to leave home after eating his breakfast, and the cow was yet unmilked, showing that the brute was in a hurry to accomplish his diabolical deed. He was put under arrest, and taken before the Justice of the district the next day. His guilt was established beyond a doubt, and a Kemper county mob promptly interposed and saved the officers of the law any further trouble about disposing of him. That is the way of the Kemper boys in dealing with devils in human form. Now, ye stalwart scoundrels, howl long, and loud, and make the most of it.—Meridian Mercury.

The people of the city of Racine were thrown into a state of unusual excitement on Friday night last by the shooting of one of their most prominent citizens, Capt. W. R. Pugh. Capt. Pugh was captain of the schooner Rainbow, and reputed to have been worth a considerable fortune. He was much respected by the community in Racine. It seems that a walking match took place on that evening at Belle City Hall between Higgie, of Racine, and one Dammars, of Chicago, Higgie winning the race; that Capt. Pugh and Hardy Clifford, of Milwaukee, wagered $175 on the race, Pugh betting on Higgie. After the affair was over Clifford refused to allow the stakeholder, Simpson, to pay the money he had bet and lost, at the same time accusing Capt. Pugh of having bought up the two men and roping him in. There was no truth in the matter and the captain informed him to that effect and most emphatically denied it. Clifford then sneaked off and went to the Huggins House, being a little worse off for liquor. Shortly after Capt. Pugh entered the private room at the hotel and asked Ed. Simpson, the stakeholder, for the money. Simpson refused to give it up, saying that Clifford had told him not to, but advised the captain to go up stairs and see Clifford about the matter. This he did, meeting Clifford in the office and asking him to come down stairs and settle the bill. He refused to go, but the captain good naturedly caught hold of his coat and led him to the head of the stairs, when he jerked away and without the least cause or provocation pulled a revolver from his pocket and fired at Capt. Pugh, but the shot struck the wall and did no harm. Pugh then jumped and caught hold of the murderous villain, as did Arthur Cressing, but he had murder in his heart and shot again, the bullet going into the floor. He then fired two more shots in quick succession, both taking effect. Pugh then descended the stairs and was taken to his home, where he died on Saturday morning. The excitement was intense. Capt. Pugh, though somewhat of a sporting man, was very popular and had many friends, not only in Racine but in Kenosha. Clifford gave himself up to the officers and was lodged in jail. So indignant were the people that an attempt was made to lynch him; the militia was ordered out for protection, and the preliminary examination before Justice Snyder took place in the residence of the Sheriff adjacent to the jail to avoid a disastrous result. The excitement died away during Monday, still a righteous indignation exists in the minds of the Racine people and many friends throughout the state, and even now Clindon may see to it that he does not get the unceremonious execution of the law, if not of statute law, a law which an indlgnant and injured people make for themselves. MANDAN, D. T., Aug. 17.—The details of the dastardly murder committed near Ft. Lincoln were fully brought out at the coroner's inquest to-day. The evidence is conclusive that Jacob Booke was literally clubbed to death by the prisoners, John and Charles Trumbell and Ira Hall. The skull of the victim showed several terrible cracks, and a verdict charging the three men with murder in the first degree was rendered by the coroner's jury, without leaving their scats. The crime having been committed on an Indian reservation the preliminary examination will be held before a United States commissioner at Bismarck, to-morrow. Major Mitchell is conducting the prosecution in a very able manner, and has associated with him Geo. P. Flannery, of Bismarck. The sheriff is preparing to ward off a possible lynching.

SAN ANTONIO, September 29.—A gentleman, who is just up from Gonzales, furnishes the reporter with a thrilling and highly interesting account of the rescue of a negro fiend from a fierce and vengeful mob. The negro was charged with outraging the person of a 12-year-old girl, about six miles east of Gonzales. He was captured and jailed at Cuero, De Witt county. As soon as it was learned that he had been caught a mob was organized for the purpose of meting out summary justice. This reached the ears of the Cuero officials, who had the prisoner transferred to Victoria jail. He remained here a day or so, when it was learned that a mob was coming. He was then returned to Cuero and lodged in jail. Knowing that he was not safe there, and that they would have to give him up or bring about great bloodshed, he was turned over to Sergeant Rudd, of Captain Oglesby's command of state troops. Rudd took him at night, and accompanied by Deputy Sheriff Kilgore, of De Witt county, rushed him through to Gonzales, whence he was taken to Harwood. Shortly after arrival the early train passed, which Rudd boarded with his prisoner, whom he took to Waelder, leaving the impression that he was going through to Houston, but he returned from Waelder on the next train bound west, passing through a branch of the mob at Harwood, and came on to San Antonio, safely lodging his prisoner in the jail here. The entire county of Gonzales seemed anxious to get hold of the negro, and the mob hunting him numbered about 250. Sergeant Rudd states that he would like to see the negro punished for his crime, but it was his duty as an officer to protect him, that the law might take its course, and he intended doing so at any risk. The determination, self-sacrifice, and ultimate success which characterized the officer's work are almost without paralel. Here the prisoner is safe, while in Gonzales and adjacent counties the feeling was so strong that the mob would have resorted to the most desperate means to secure possession of the villain. He would probably have been burned at the stake.

Special Dispatch to THE BEE.

ATLANTA, Ga., August 9.—News reached here to-day of a riot in Eastman's, Sunday afternoon, when five persons were killed. For some days a colored excursion to a camp meeting in Eastman has been advertised in Macon and surrounding towns, with a promise that "more amusement will be furnished than at any camp meeting ever held in Georgia." There appears to have been whisky drinking and gambling in the vicinity of the camp meeting and a victim complaining to Marshal Buchanan of the loss of his watch, taken by Jake Johnson.

A NOTORIOUS COLORED GAMBLER, the marshal, with deputy Harral, went to arrest Johnson, who knocked the deputy down and ran. The marshal opened fire and killed him, which so incensed the negroes that they clamored for revenge. Seeing a white man running through a grove toward the deputy's house, they made after him. The mob tore down the fence, and securing the palings as weapons, made a demand of the occupants of the house to surrender. A young man named James Harvard, of Cochian, who accompanied the excursion, secreted himself under the house, but was discovered, dragged out and beaten over the head with the palings, and then the negroes put a pistol to his head and

BLEW HIS BRAINS OUT.

After Harvard was dead the infuriated mob continued to beat his body and mashed his skull. The citizens of Eastman armed themselves and a general engagement took place, in which three negroes were killed and several persons wounded on both sides, the negroes being routed. When the excursionists started home in the afternoon the rioters were still boisterous, and had a general row in the passenger coach. A negro cut his wife to pieces, pistols were drawn all around, and the conductor in attempting to eject the man who did the cutting was

THROWN FROM THE PLATFORM with him, and his life was in imminent peril until he secured a coupling link and knocked the desperado senseless. The rioters cut the bell line of the train, but the engineer discovering their purpose pulled out the engine lever and ran into Macon, making the fastest time on record on that road. Numerous arrests were made, the principals being caught, and quiet has been temporarily restored, although the citizens of the town in which Harvard lived have organized, and the lynching of the rioters is apprehended.

ATLANTA, GA., September 7.—Last week negroes who had been engaged in a riot that occurred in Dodge county recently, were being tried. Eleven negroes were sent to the penitentiary for life, and five have been sentenced to death on the gallows. Those who got to the penitentiary for their way to the coal mines of Senator Brown, in North Georgia. Among those sentenced to death is Ella Moore, a negro woman, who is said to have been a leader of the outbreak.

A Dozen More are Awaiting Trial.
Indignation about Eastman is so great because all of the prisoners were not sentenced to be hung that the penitentiary guard had to steal away in the night with his captives. While passing a station a short distance from Eastman twelve men, armed with shotguns, stood on the bank for the purpose of firing upon the prisoners as the train passed. Learning of their being there before the train reached that point the conductor instructed the engineer to put on a full head of steam while passing. This was done, and the gauntlet was run in that way.

Saving the Lives of All on Board.
Had the train slacked up the prisoners would have been shot and killed without doubt. Jolly Colonel Jack Brown, brown and effervescent, has turned up in Washington again, and was to-day interviewed by one of the inquisitive reporters of THE CRITIC.

“Where’ve ye been, Kurnel?” THE CRITIC asked, adopting McKee Rankin’s old “49” dialect.

“I have been in Georgia for the past seven weeks.

“Politics down thar is boomin’, I ’spose ?”

“Yes, sir, everything in politics seems lovely; that is, the Democrats are weakening, and there is a strong probability of Stephens’ defeat for Governor. Independent Republicans and Greenbackers have united against bossism and ring Democracy, and we believe there will be such a change in the October and November elections as will astonish the nation. Many Republicans and anti-Bourbons will be elected to the Legislature, and there will be a change in our Congressional delegation.”

“You didn’t get the Congressional nomination, it appears,” THE CRITIC remarked seriocomically.

“No, I did not get the nomination for Congress in my district, but I did much better; that is, I succeeded in concentrating the entire Republican vote on Judge Harrell, the Independent anti-Bourbon candidate. The Judge is a man of good character, splendid ability, and for four years presided over the Superior Court of the Pataulo circuit. Hundreds of Democrats will vote for him; besides there are three thousand more Republican voters than Democratic in my District. My party is thoroughly organized and all its members will vote for Judge Harrell; hence I believe that the old Third will be represented by an anti-Bourbon in the Forty-eighth Congress.”

“You’ve been busy, then, during your absence?”
"You've been busy, then, during your absence?"
"Yes. Although I have done some good work for the past few weeks, yet I shall be on hand in October to render Judge Harrell all the assistance in my power."
"You are back just in time for the latest sensation."
"Yes; I have returned just in time to participate in the excitement created by the verdict in the Star-Route case. As to what I think about those cases I have this to say. I have thought about and studied that Star-Route matter a great deal, and have always expressed the opinion that no jury could legally convict those defendants. Much time and money have been wasted on them. The idea of taking up the time of the Courts and country more than three months in trying one case is preposterous. Why, sir, I have defended more than sixty murderers since the 6th day of last August. I know it seems impossible, but it is, nevertheless, true as gospel. Such anoteer trial for murder cannot be found in the annals of the courts, nor in the history of the world, as that at Eastman.
"What were the facts?"
"Well, the history of it is this: On the 6th day of last August two excursion trains emptied two thousand colored people at a camp-meeting in the little village of Eastman. Most of the excursionists were drinking or drunk, as well as armed with pistols, knives or razors. About two p. m. of that day the marshal and his deputy of the village arrested one of their number for stealing a watch. While taking him to jail the prisoner attempted to escape and was killed.

"Finally two or three hundred of them espied a young man running away from the main street, and supposing him to be the Marshal fleeing from their threat and vengeance, they began chase at full speed, sending after the fugitive a hundred pistol balls, two or three of which took effect. The young man, after running four hundred yards took refuge in the house of a friend. The infuriated negroes, lead by one woman only, brick-batted, fired into the house and finally entered. Young Mr. Harvard, the fugitive, an innocent young man, a stranger in the town, exhausted and wounded by the infuriated mob, was found. The mob beat him with sticks, cut him, shot him through the head and killed him. This satisfied their thirst for blood. They had killed one white man—got even, and dispersed. In less than twenty-four hours the jail was full of negroes charged with the murder of James Q. Harvard. I was the only lawyer in that section of the State who would accept an appointment from the court to defend them. More than sixty were tried before the commitment court. Many were turned loose upon failing to identify. In the meanwhile Judge Pate called an extra session of the Superior Court to specially try the men confined in jail. On the 22d of the same month (August) we selected a jury and put on trial ten of the twenty-six. The result was six of that number will be hung on the 26th of next month, and the other four were sent to the penitentiary for life. The result of these trials was as follows: On Tuesday, the 17th of August, ten of the defendants were put on trial in one batch, viz: Ella Moore, Reddick Powell, Bob Donelson, Joe King, Simon O'Gwinn alias O'Quinn, Isaac Shipman, Henry Howell, Jack Knoles, John Kellam and Robert Stith. After a trial that lasted five days, these were all found guilty of murder in the second degree. The last four were recommended to life imprisonment in the penitentiary. The first six were sentenced by Judge Pate to explain the crime of which they were convicted upon the scaffold on the 20th of October, between the hours of 11 o'clock a. m. and 3 o'clock p. m., privately, in the town of Eastman, and in the meantime were sent to Bibb county jail for safe keeping. These were the strongest cases, and it is thought that among them is included the one who actually did the shooting that was the immediate cause of Mr. Harvard's death, while it is certain that they include those who took the most active part in the riot from its inception to its tragic end.

Then seven others charged and indicted for the same offense were put upon trial, to wit: Daniel Bryant, Robert, Robert, Gus Gibbs, Robert George, Robert, Best, James Oliver Copeland, Frank Adams, and William McRae. Their trial lasted four or five days, and the jury, after a searching investigation, rendered a verdict against all of the defendants for murder in the second degree, recommending them to imprisonment in the penitentiary for life. In the next and last batch there were five prisoners tried together, viz: Stafford Foster, Robert Parish, George Frink, Henry Carmichael and Jim Grlswold, with the same result as in the cases of the last preceding seven. In this case Judge Mershon presided for Judge Pate. The State was represented in the trials of the rioters by J. M. Stubbs of Dublin, Solicitor General Eason, J. F. DeLacy, E. Herrman, and Roberts & Smith, of Eastman. The defendants were represented by Colonel Jack Brown, of Americus; J. Bishop, Jr., of Eastman; J. W. Haygood, of Montezuma; Courtland Symmes, of Brunswick, and T. C. Taylor, of Hawkinsville. The investigations were long and tedious. The prisoners had a perfectly fair and impartial trial. But the evidence against them was strong, and could not be rebutted or overcome. Some of those who were sent to the penitentiary for life may well thank their stars that they were so fortunate as to save their necks. It is true, in the cases of two or three of those who were recommended to the mercy of the court and sentenced to the penitentiary, the evidence was mostly circumstantial, but the links in the chain of circumstances were strong and well connected. In all the cases but two or three, however, the testimony left no peg upon which to hang a reasonable doubt as to the guilt of the parties. The writer knows whereof he speaks, for he was present at the trials, connected with the cases as counsel for the defendants, and has a brief of the evidence now before him.

The August special term of the court, held for the purpose of trying the rioters, was an important as well as an expensive one to Dodge county. Besides the indictment and conviction of twenty-one men and one woman, six of whom, including the woman, for murder, were sentenced to death to answer for their crime, bills of indictment were also returned against J. B. A. Buchan and A. P. Harrell for manslaughter; and a large number of bills were found against parties for smaller offenses, amounting only to misdemeanors.

This special term of the court cost our county about $7,000 in extra taxes, besides the individual expenses and inconveniences to our citizens. For several weeks there was a stagnation in trade and business of every kind; farmers and business men from all parts of the county were called away from their homes to attend court as jurors and witnesses to the great neglect and suffering of their private affairs.

Since the court adjourned many of our citizens have been in constant suspense in anticipation of more trouble, owing to numerous wild rumors that have been circulated to the effect that the colored people intended to interfere with the course of law and justice, and make an attempt to prevent the execution of the six rioters convicted of murder and sentenced to be hanged. Even while the court was yet in session, Judge Pate received an anonymous postal card from Macon, signed "Somebody," and threatening his life. The Atlanta Defiance, a newspaper published by negroes, in its issue of September 19th, contained an editorial outrageously attacking the court and juries that tried the rioters, stating that they were convicting innocent colored men by the wholesale (all of which was unqualified false), and calling upon the colored people generally to know whether they would tamely submit to such a procedure. The Savannah Echo, another newspaper edited by negroes, copied this shameful article and gave it still further circulation. Again, recently, the Echo published another editorial in its own columns scurrillous in its character, and calculated to incite the negroes to some act of violence and interference with the verdict of the jury and order of the court convicting the rioters and sentencing them to be hung. A few days ago another anonymous postal card was mailed at the post office here, directed to "Mr. Everybody, By G—d, Eastman, Ga." and threatening trouble on the day of the hanging, saying that when those negroes are hung "we will all die together." There have also been various rumors of secret meetings held by the negroes, plotting to rescue the prisoners. Last week Sheriff Sapp received a letter from the jailer in Macon stating that he was informed that the negroes there were organized to prevent the prisoners from being brought down and executed; that it was rumored that an attempt would be made to rescue them between here and Macon, by tearing up the railroad track and wrecking the train upon which they were to be brought down, and that there would probably be a thousand negroes here on the day of the execution from Dodge's railroad in Telfair county, and other places, to play the mischief generally.

In view of all these things, for the protection and safety of our town, for the preservation of order, and to maintain the majesty of the law and carry out the mandates of the court, our citizens organized themselves into a quasi military company to assist the Sheriff in case he needed assistance; the Town Council was recommended to put several extra policemen on duty at night, and to put on a strong force on the day of the execution, and the Sheriff summoned a posse of a hundred and fifty or two hundred men from the county for guard duty to-day.

Sheriff Sapp saw that trouble was brewing, and that his own life was in imminent peril, for the negroes were already beginning to make threats and talk of revenge, saying that they had four men to one white man, and if they didn't take the advantage of it they ought to have their d—d throats cut.

The dead body of Jake Terrapin was removed to the platform in front of Sheriff Sapp's store, on County Road street, where a riotous mob rapidly gathered around it. The fury increased. There were loud cries for revenge because a colored man had been killed. A mob caught Harrell, the Deputy Marshal, near the post office, cut him severely with their knives, and would certainly have butchered him had not Mr. James Q. Harvard, a worthy young white man of Cochran, who happened to be in Eastman that day, passed by just at that untimely moment. By some means or other the attention of the mob was directed to him, and they were made to believe that he was the Marshal, and that they had the wrong man, as it seems that it was the Marshal and his deputy they wanted to kill. They immediately let Harrell go and went like so many bloodthirsty madmen after Mr. Harvard, chasing him several hundred yards with knives, clubs, brickbats, hatchets, pistols, etc., yelling and shooting and swearing vengeance every step of the way. But here language is inadequate to picture what occurred. The scene fairly beggars description. An infuriated mob of two or three hundred colored people surrounded the premises. Sticks and palings torn from the fence were waved in the air, brickbats were hurled into the hallway; the blades of knives and razors glistened in the sunlight; pistols were fired into and under the house; the gate and fence were pulled down. The Eastman Hanging.
Yesterday there was enacted at Eastman, Dodge county, a scene which we believe has never been enacted before in Georgia, and let us devoutly hope may never have to be witnessed again. Five murderers—four men and one woman—were hung all at the same time to satisfy the just and stern demands of the law.

The crime for which these culprits suffered is fully detailed in all its horrible ghastliness in our telegraphic columns. It was indeed a bloody, cruel murder which these wretches, as ringleaders of a drunken and excited mob, caused to be committed upon the person of an innocent man against whom they, while inflamed with drink, had raised a cause less hue and cry. The outrageous crime would have amply justified the citizens of Eastman in taking the law in their own hands—if lynch law is ever justifiable—and making short work of the rioters and murderers on the spot. But, to the credit of those citizens be it spoken, they determined to let justice take its course. The offenders against the law were promptly arrested, fairly tried and duly sentenced in proportion to the enormity of their respective crimes. Fifteen were sent to the penitentiary—most of them for life—while six were found worthy of death.

Notwithstanding, too, that the condemned received fair trials, and the righteousness of their various sentences was not disputed, it was resolved by the Executive of this State that nothing should be left undone to mete out to them simple justice. To this end, although their counsel made no plea in their behalf after conviction, the Governor made it a special point to examine thoroughly into the evidence against them to see whether or not any extenuating circumstances existed which would justify executive clemency. After diligent investigation, however, the sentences of all save one were found to be richly deserved, and in the case of this one, Isaac Shipman, a reprieve was granted for thirty days. If, in the meantime, it be ascertained that there were any palliative conditions connected with his crime, his sentence will in all probability be commuted to imprisonment.

It will be seen, therefore, that the five criminals who yesterday suffered the extreme penalty of the law in Eastman were, notwithstanding the heinousness and horrible cold-bloodiness of their deed, granted every possible chance. They had forfeited their lives to the majesty of the law, and both justice and the well being of society demanded their execution. Their fate should be a lasting warning to the evil-minded and evil-disposed hereafter. EASTMAN, Ga., Oct. 20.—At 1 o'clock to-day Riddick Powell, Simon O'Guinn, Joseph King, Robert Donaldson, and Ella Moore, negroes, were hanged in the jail yard for murder and riot. No attempt was made to rescue them, and not more than fifty negroes, from whom violence was expected, were in the town. Military from Macon were present.

The crime they expiated was the flendish murder of a young white man named James Q. Harvard of Cochran, during a colored camp meeting at Eastman. On Sunday, Aug. 6, special trains were run to the camp from Macon and Jesup. The attendance of colored people was large, and a number of young white men were among the excursionists, including young Harvard. At the camp grounds the negroes indulged freely in whiskey and gambling. Among the sharpers who attended was Jake Johnson, a notorious character, who fleeced a number of the colored people, and took a watch and chain from one of them. The theft was reported to Marshal Buchan, who endeavored to arrest Jake, but the latter fled, and was pursued by the marshal and his deputy, Peter Harrell. Both fired shots at him, the deputy hitting and killing him instantly. The negroes became excited. They carried Jake's body to the camp grounds, where the women became loud in their lamentations and exclamations. Women and men were soon all wrought up to such a pitch of excitement that the men began to fire shots in the air. Suddenly in their frenzy they started to find Marshal Buchan and Deputy Harrell. In their search they saw a white man running through a grove of trees, and soon they were in hot pursuit. The man ran in the direction of the residence of W. W. Harrell, which he entered. The negroes surrounded the house, while five of them entered and secured James Q. Harvard, whom they mistook for the marshal's deputy. They took the young man from the house, and, tearing off pickets from the fence, beat him horribly. One placed a pistol at his head, and ended his agonies. Even after death the negroes continued to belabor the body.

They then went into the town in search of Marshal Buchan, but were met by the citizens, who had armed themselves. THE END OF A SPREE.

SHOT INTO MARRIAGE.

KNIFED FOR A WOMAN.

John Tribbett, a boy fifteen years of age, was arrested at the levee Thursday morning by Sheriff Butler, of Ottertail county, Minn., and lodged in our county jail. He is charged with the murder of two men at Perham, in the county mentioned. The circumstances of the murder are given below. They were gleaned from a telegram received at the Tribune office yesterday. It appears that on Monday, the 30th ult., that a surveyor who came up there from Michigan, started out about that time to survey some land located several miles from that town, and took with him a German boy named Fritz, belonging to that vicinity. While out they were joined by a lad named John Tribbett, aged fifteen, a boy of quarrelsome and bad character, who had been working in the woods during the winter. Tribbett was well known, but regarded as a worthless vagabond. On Monday Tribbett borrowed a gun from a neighbor, who shortly afterwards heard some shots, but thought nothing of it. Later Tribbett came into town with the surveyor's watch and a revolver. He sold the watch for five dollars to the city marshal. It is supposed that on the same night or Tuesday morning he left for the west, which supposition has proven well founded. On Friday the dead body of the German boy Fritz was discovered by a farmer, the head crushed in, several bullet holes in the body, and a fatal knife wound in the neck. This led to a search for the surveyor, whose body was found that evening. The young villian arrived here last Saturday evening and went under the alias of Ford. When he left the scene of the murder he had about $90, but upon arriving here he was broke, as on yesterday he pawned a revolver to John Ludwig and then proceeded to the levee, and while engaged in a conversation with the captain of the ferry boat Undine the officer rode on the steamer and captured his game. A reporter for the TRIBUNE called at the jail last evening and had an interview with the prisoner. He appeared cheerful and gave the turnkey a cigar. The writer informed him that he desired his statement of the affair with which he was charged, and upon a moments reflection replied that according to his experience statements were only made to lawyers by big men, and he thought he would imitate his seniors. But after being assured that it would not prejudice his case by claiming his innocence, he still insisted upon refusing, which in itself was a confession of guilt.

Young Tribbett, who is only fifteen years and one month old, is as villainous a specimen of a dime novel reader as one could discover in a year's hunt. He is large, coarse and brutal in appearance.

During a conversation with Geo. Thomas, the jailor, the TRIBUNE was informed by that gentleman that the murderer had confessed to him to the extent that he was not alone in the murder, that the blame was not all on him. He is evidently the one wanted.

The information that has come into the possession of the TRIBUNE regarding the boy, John Tibbitts, who was arrested in this city Monday, charged with the murder of two men at Perham, Minn., proves him to be the most brutal human fiend that ever walked the earth. At the jail Monday night he told the prisoners that had his gun not been in soak, the officer who arrested him would have gone back to Perham in a box. And while in the car Wednesday morning, by which he went east, he remarked to the conductor: "For Jesus Christ's sake, conductor, shut that door and charge an admission fee, and when we reach Fargo we'll have a bully good time." He admitted that he didn't expect to live long after reaching the scene of the murder.

About dusk last Thursday evening, John Watson and Cash Austin, railroad hands employed in grading near Billingsley's, shot and robbed William Fox, a fellow-laborer, of over $200, at a point about 10 miles below Patton's station. Fox was wounded in the wrist and side, but made his way to Hale, Smith & Co.'s camp, where he related what had occurred. A strong posse was immediately raised to pursue the robbers, which, after an all-night chase, succeeded in capturing them to Hale, Smith & Co.'s camp, them to Hale, Smith & Co.'s camp, where they were identified by Fox. A court was improvised, and the prisoners put upon trial. The evidence was clear against John Watson. He had been a "partner" of Fox's for months past, sleeping and eating with him, and fired the shots at Fox as the latter was walking ahead of him, on his way back from the Kelton road crossing, where he had been to purchase some underclothes and a pair of overalls.

Austin had at first refused to assist Watson, but the latter compelled him to help by threatening to kill him.

Watson and Austin worked on the grade only at intervals, when they got broke. Their avocation was that of "sagebrush gamblers," and they followed the railroad camps from Granger out.

CINCINNATI, O., July 20.—Catherine Higgins, aged 25 years, while driving geese from a railroad track, was killed by an engine.

A Panic in Tripoli.

LONDON, June 20.—The panic among the Christians in Tripoli is increasing.

A Centenarian's Death.

MARIETTA, O., July 20.—John Springer, aged 108 years, died of old age.

Resignation Accepted.

PARIS, July 20.—Grevy has accepted Goblet's resignation.

Arizona Indian War.

The following has been received at the War Department:

"PRESIDIO OF SAN FRANCISCO, July 19, 1882.

"To Adjutant-General, Washington, D. U.:

"The Commanding General, Department of Arizona, reports as follows: That Captain Chaffee, in command of detachments of the Third and Sixth Cavalry, overtook the hostile on the 17th on the west branch of Chevelon's Fork, eight miles north of General's Springs, and held them till the Apache column came up, when a severe fight ensued in a deep ravine, managed by Captain Chaffee, lasting till night.

"The Indians fled in the night leaving six dead. Scouts report twenty killed; six women and children were captured; also thirty-two head of stock and all their camp equipage and traps. The troops lost one enlisted man and one scout killed. Lieutenants Converse and Morgan, Third Cavalry, and five men were wounded, to dangerously. The hostiles were led by Nautithis, one of the Cibicu prisoners, and consisted of other released prisoners and renegade scouts. Mason's command joined Chaffee in the night, and must be in pursuit of fugitives.

"MCDOWELL, Major-General."

noah-parks-winston-county-1882-07-19.A10: A COLORED preacher of Mississippi has been lynched by his neighbors because "he stole corn." His offense justified the punishment. The peculiar and exclusive field of thieving operations of the negro minister is the hen-house. In a sense he is licensed to steal chickens, for the world recognizes the fact that the affinity of hens and negroes is something that cannot be overcome. It is popularly accepted as a truth that a black preacher can no more avoid prowling about henroosts than he can fly when the power to do so would be most advantageous to him. This being so the owners of hens are disposed to bottle their wrath at the loss of fowls when they are aware of the proximity of a colored minister. When one of these dispensers of the gospel becomes so immoral as to stray from his natural and recognized field of operations, and steals corn, there seems no other course left than to promptly lynch him.

DOMESTIC.
MRS. ABRAHAM LINCOLN died at Springfield, Illinois, July 16. Mrs. Lincoln had a great sense of wrong, not only in the loss of her husband, but in the treatment she has received from the world since that event. She spent a good deal of time in Europe in a wandering, aimless way, seeking impossible health and consolation for cureless wounds. Mrs. Lincoln was a Kentucky lady, Her family was one of distinction. She has relatives living in this neighborhood, Mrs. Kellogg, her half-sister, and Mrs. Judge Dickson, her cousin. Her only surviving child is Robert Todd Lincoln, the Secretary of War.

FIFTEEN thousand persons assembled at Madison Square Garden, New York, July 17, to witness a glove fight between John Sullivan, of Boston, and Tug Wilson, of England. The conditions of the fight were: Sullivan should knock his opponent out of time in four rounds, failing to do which, the Englishman, though knocked down twenty-seven times in about fifteen minutes, was declared to be the winner. Wilson looked like a pigmy beside his opponent, but to win the money, stuck and received all the pounding Sullivan could give him.

Fifty-nine horses and a cow were burned in a Chicago livery stable on the 17th.

A hailstorm at St. Joseph, Mo., caused a loss aggregating $50,000.

"Tug" Wilson's share of the gate receipts at the glove contest between himself and Sullivan, in New York, on the 17th, together with the $1,000 stakes won, was $12,700.

A little child named Hoffman fell in a cistern near Upper Sandusky, Ohio. The mother rang the farm bell for help, and then sprang into the cistern. When assistance arrived, both mother and child were dead.

Two men were killed and six colored laborers wounded, in a riot between laborers on the Cincinnati and Georgia Railroad, near Rockmont, Georgia.

A boat containing Dr. Addison F. King and wife, of London, Ohio, was capsized in Lake Chautauqua, and both were drowned.

A two-year-old child of Nelvin Smith, a wealthy Montreal merchant, has been abducted, and a ransom of $50,000 demanded on penalty of the child's life.

Dr. Keys was released from an insane asylum at St. Joe, Mo., where he had been confined two years, after having killed Dr. Roberts, of Millville. The next day Keys went to Millville, against the advice of his friends, where the son of the murdered Roberts saw him and killed him with a pistol shot.

In the Court-house at Floyd, La., David I. Norwood attempted to cane L. J. Polk, both prominent planters. Each pulled Colt's dragoon pistols and began firing. Polk was shot dead, and Norwood was badly wounded.

Six lives were lost by the sinking of the steamer John Wilson, near New Orleans.

The United States Iron and Tin Plate Company, of Tuckersport, Pennsylvania, has failed; liabilities $150,000.

Destructive forest fires are reported raging between East Tawas and Au Sable Mich.

Many persons were injured by flying missiles in a storm in the vicinity of Lancaster, Penn., on the 19th.

Of a party of seven persons two women and one man were drowned in Portage River, near Houghton, Mich.

The funeral of the late Mrs. Lincoln took place at Springfield, Ill., July 19. An immense throng was present, but services were conducted in a quiet manner. An eloquent discourse was delivered by Mrs. Lincoln's pastor, Rev. Mr. Reed.

Three children were fatally poisoned by some unknown person in Northampton County, Virginia.

The estimated wheat crop of Kansas this year is 35,000,000 bushels.

A dispatch on the 20th inst. said the ship Theobold, with crew of nineteen, sailing from Philadelphia for San Francisco, was supposed to be lost.

The Naval Court of Inquiry holds no one responsible for the loss of the Arctic steamer Rodgers.

By Court decision women are eligible to admission as attorneys in Connecticut.

A shock of earthquake was felt at Cairo, Illinois, July 20.

In Winston County, Mississippi, a colored preacher suspected of stealing corn,

was hanged by a mob several times by the thumbs and finally by the neck, until he was almost dead, and was cut down by friends just in time to resuscitate him. The New York Hebrew Emigrant Aid Society, on July 20, returned to Europe fifteen Russian Hebrew families who are physically and mentally unable to earn a livelihood in this country. Hereafter the society will not permit pauper Hebrews to be landed at New York. FIFTEEN fatal cases of lockjaw, caused by wounds from toy pistols July 4, have been reported in Chicago, three in the country. Six boys died in Burlington and three in Peoria.

PERSONAL AND POLITICAL.

General Grant has been giving his opinion upon the Eastern question to a Philadelphia Record reporter. He sides with England, and believes an English protectorate would help develop the resources of the country and improve the condition of the people.

Colonel Calvin Morgan, brother of the famous General John Morgan, died at Lexington, Kentucky, July 19.

The New York Greenback Labor party has nominated Epenatus Howe for Governor, and the rest of the State ticket. Resolutions declare that the Civil Service demands all officials to be elected instead of appointed.

The Texas Democrats nominated Judge Ireland for Governor by acclamation.

The Star Route men are discouraged in the probability of John A. Walsh's testimony being admitted by Judge Wylie. It is understood that the decision of this question will affect the admissibility of the Rerdell confession, upon which depends the success of the prosecution's efforts to make out a case against the defendants.

Wm. WILLIAMSON, arrested on the charge of larceny from the files of the Attorney-General's office of a large number of letters written by Daniel Webster and others, has been dismissed, the prosecution entering a nolle prosequi.

At Columbus, Ohio, on the 20th, Clark Irvine, of Mt. Vernon, was elected Chairman of the Democratic State Central Committee, and John G. Thompson Chairman of the State Executive Committee. The vote for Thompson was fourteen, to seven for Si Hoffman, of Cincinnati.

FANNY PARNELL, sister of Charles Stewart Parnell, died suddenly at Old Ironsides, Bordentown, New Jersey, July 20, from paralysis of the heart.

MRS. SCoville protests in court at Washington against the probate of Guiteau's will.

GEORGE H. INKOFF, a soldier under the great Napoleon, died at Richmond, Indiana, July 20, aged 107 years.

IN THE Georgia Democratic Convention, July 20, Hon. A. H. Stephens was nominated for Governor; N. C. Barnett, Secretary of State; W A. Wright, Comptroller General; D. N. Speer, Treasurer; Clifford Anderson, Attorney General; Thomas Hardeman, Congressman-at-large. J. B. THE United States Fish Commission has made a special report to Congress, which will be the most exhaustive work on food fishes ever printed. It will make three quarto volumes of eight hundred pages each, and be profusely illustrated.

At a meeting of the Ohio Republican Association in Washington, D. C., the other night, a letter from Mrs. Garfield, offering to sell the family residence, at the corner of Thirteenth and I street, was read. She set forth that she preferred to have the place fall into the hands of such an association, which would cherish it for the memories connected with it, rather than let it go to some private party who might alter it. She said that Gen. Garfield had told her once that it was worth $18,000, but she would take $15,000 for it. Real estate dealers value the property at $9,000.

The glove-fight between Wilson and Sullivan in New York City on the 17th lasted fifteen minutes, and was witnessed by an immense throng. Wilson won the money.

EMILIANO DANIEL and Alejo Zespeda, with fifty followers, surprised the town of Tomala, Las Chiapas, on the 17th, and after a stubborn fight released all the prisoners in the jail, who were armed and pressed into the ranks. Captain Guzman, with eighty Mexican soldiers, charged the revolutionists and put them to flight.

It seems that Oscar Goodwin, cashier of the Logansport (Ind.) Bank, who disappeared some time ago, taking with him his bond, and tearing from the records all reference to it, is a defaulter to the amount of $15,000, the whole sum being in account of the Merchants' National Bank of Chicago.

While confirmation services were in progress in the Kentucky Penitentiary the other day a number of convicts in the hemp house were secreting hammers, saws, files, and other instruments likely to be of service in effecting their escape. The timely arrival of a guard spoiled the plot.

THE list of victims of the toy pistol in the vicinity of Boston since July 4 has swollen to forty, and Cincinnati reports six deaths within a few days from the same cause.

In Buenos Ayres, during services in memory of Garibaldi, a curtain in a public hall took fire, producing a stampede. A wall toppled over on the assemblage, and twenty bodies have been taken from the ruins.

At Millville, Mass., the other day, Joseph Garbwree had a fight of twenty minutes' duration with a black-snake twelve feet in length, and received ten bites.

Miss Greyson, of Erie, Pa., who for many years had been confined to her bed with spinal disease, recently made arrangements for simultaneous prayer in her behalf, and at the hour fixed sprang up healed. It happened, however, that no prayer-meeting was held.

Mexico was agitated by an earthquake the other day. The shock was particularly trying in the capital, where the people went on their knees in the streets and the greatest consternation prevailed.

The engine of a gravel train plunged into the river at Niles, Mich., on the 19th. The driver and firemen were seriously injured.

A number of men broke into the house of Noah Parks, a colored preacher, in Winston County, Miss., July 19, dragged him out of bed, put a rope round his neck, and strung him up to a tree. Friends cut him down and resuscitated him the moment the lynchers left. The reverend gentleman was suspected of stealing corn.

Col. Philipon, accused of participation in a Nihilistic conspiracy at St. Petersburg, has been exiled to Siberia.

Mr. A. Forcas, the Vicksburg (Miss.) store-keeper who invented the burglar sensation the other day, is not only charged with murdering his wife and burning his store and dwelling, but testimony is being accumulated to prove that he is also guilty of the assassination of a negro drayman several months since.

LANCASTER, Pa., and vicinity was swept by a storm on the 19th. Many persons were injured and much property destroyed. Boston, Mass., was flooded by heavy rains on the same day.

A GREAT fire raged in Smyrna, Asia Minor, on the 19th. Fourteen hundred houses were destroyed and 6,000 people are homeless.

OFFICERS of the steamer John Wilson, sunk in the Atchafalaya River the other night, report the loss of fifteen lives.

W. B. Johnston, sheriff of Winston county, in this State, has resigned his office on account of financial embarrassment.

Col. Beverly Matthews, a lawyer of Columbus, and a prominent man in this State, died last week.

Dr. Sowers and Hartigan, two of the committee appointed to examine Guiteau's brain, report it in a generally healthy state.

Judge Black says Gen. Hancock will be the next nominee of the Democratic party for President. The New York Sun prefers Black, and Seymour says Tilden is the man if he wants it.

Julienne Neville, a grandson of the revolutionary Gen. Daniel Morgan, and for fifty years a prominent man in Louisiana political and social life, died in New Orleans on the 20th.

A white physician of Portland, Oregon, was recently called by a Spokano Indian to treat his son on Klamath reservation. The boy died and the father shot the physician and fled.

People should not wonder at the scarcity of good servant girls, because if they are good for anything, its sure to be found out and they are soon married.

Texas Siftings says, up in Missouri they are just beginning to break themselves of the habit of holding up their hands every time a stranger enters the car.

An exchange says: "Put oat meal in your ice water." Well, we have heard it called various names before, but we must contess that "oat meal" is new to us.

At a convention of Land Leaguers in Philadelphia, it was decided to make the watermelon Ireland's national emblem, because it has the green above the red.

Two Rochester maidens, enjoying Silver Lake, telegraphed their father; "Come and bring Bess." He came, and with him several kegs of pale Bohemian lager. The telegram read beer instead of Bess. The mistake was taken in, of course, and so was the beer.

It is serenely claimed by a Bradford editor, that a young lady in charge of a local telephone office has such dulcet tones, that when she is talking through the instrument the wire between the stations becomes an Eolian harp, and little birds fly out to roost on the line in order to learn new music for their songs.

At an eastern revival meeting, the minister, in the course of his remarks, informed his hearers that he was conductor of a salvation train; the accommodations were first-class; that there were no misplaced switches to fear, and that Peter was waiting to receive them at the depot at the other end of the line. Thereupon a tall, giant, keen-visaged man in the outskirts of the crowd, addressing the clergyman, said: "I'm a good deal consarned in what you hev to say, stranger, and if you can git me a back seat on enny of them air keepers for half price, I'll buy a ticket.

"What is the matter, old fellow? you seem worried." "Well, I'm—I'm being dunned up hifi and down dale by my infernal creditors." "Oh you owe a large sum of money?" "No, but a great many small sums, and depts are like children—the smaller they are the more bother they are."

Passenger No. 4, which left Columbus at 11:55 a.m., ran into the cab car of freight train No. 12 going west, at Butler Wednesday afternoon. The accident was caused by train No. 12 falling to clear the main line. The damage was very light, only a few planks of the cab being broken. No one was hurt. Both trains were on schedule time.

There is talk in Bainbridge of introducing the electric light.

A company is reported to have been formed in Athens for the purpose of building a grain elevator and a cotton seed oil mill.

A murder was committed on board the stunner Chattahooochee just as she was moving off from the wharf at Apalachicola Monday. A white man named George Avriett, without any seeming provocation, walked up to another named Engel, who was sea'ed on an oyster barrel, placed his pistol at Engel's temple and blew his brains out. The murderer dropped the pistol, put his hands in his pockets, and was walking quietly off when rubbed. Both men are from Liberty county, Ga.

The house of Mr. S. C. Evans, a few miles above Jonesboro, was, with its contents, destroyed by fire last Saturday evening.

On last Saturday night Mr. Milton Jones, of Dublin, detected a sneak thief endeavoring to break into his smoke house. Mr. J. saluted him with three shots, which caused him to samper away, leaving a trail of blood for some distance. But in spite of his wounds he escaped before Mr. Jones could overhaul or enogolize him.

A little boy named Hyde, living in Coweta county, was bitten on the toe a few days ago. His body became very much swollen, and he suffered great muscular pain. Skillful treatment, however, saved his life.

The storehouse of Smith Bros. in Monroe county, was bursed a few night ago, with all its contents.

Commissioner Henderson still thinks that the cotton crop will be small.

Reports received at the Department of Agriculture show that an unusually large grain crop will be grown this year.

It is hinted that the present owners of the McHerson Barracks property will offer the State twelve acres of ground as a site for the proposed new capital.

The blackboard in the office of the Principal Keeper of the Penitentiary shows that so far this month there have been sixteen discharges, two escapes, one pardon granted and six new convicts received.

Officers looked after the person who fired the shot, but failed to find any clue as to whence it came or anything about it.

He was carried home, and an examination showed it to be a simple fracture. It was speedily set, and he will doubtless be able to be out again soon.

General Toombs does not agree with Attorney General Anderson in his opinion as to the invalidity of the lessees of the State road.

simon-woods-bayou-cocodrie-1882-05-16.A5: Simon Woods, a colored desperado, was killed by deputy sheriff E. A. McKinney, at Wilson's sawmill on Bayou Cocodrie, about 8 o'clock last Tuesday evening. Woods, by his own statement, was a refugee from the parish of St. Martin, where he had committed some crime. He was in jail here last year for carrying concealed weapons. Not long since he took away from one Anderson Stewart, another colored man living at Wilson's sawmill, his thirteen year year old daughter. A few daws ago the girl's mother got her her back home. Woods came there, threw the mother down, and was was attempting to cut her throat with a knife, when Stewart knocked or pulled him off. Woods then "went for him," but he he escaped into house and fastened the doors against him. He made violent efforts to break in, with threats to kill, ect., but was finally persuaded to desist and go away. Steward came to Opelousas last Tuesday, and made an affidavit against Woods; and he would not return home until an officer was sent to arrest Woods, and he advised that more than two men be sent to make the arrest, as Woods had sworn that he would not be arrested by the sheriff nor anybody else, and that he would be certain to kill at least two men with the double barrel gun which he carried. Woods waited at Stewart's cabin for him to return, threatening that he would kill him. When deputy sheriff McKinney arrived there Tuesday, Stewart retired to the woods with his gun. He was told that he could not capture him with a pistol, whereupon he procured a gun; and to induce Woods, who was no doubt watching near by, to come in from the woods, McKinney changed clothes with some one at the mill, and went to work in his place, while he mounted McKinney's horse and rode off. This strategem had the desired effect. Woods came to the mill office, set his gun down, and stated to those present that he wanted this matter (between Stewart and himself) settled. McKinney who was behind the building, made his appearance, and informed Woods that he was his prisoner. Woods sprang to his gun and seized it. McKinney told him to keep his hands off the gun, or he would shoot him. This having no effect, he covered Woods, and as he jerked up his gun he fired. Woods fell mortally wounded, the entire charge of shot making one hole through his body, on one side about the lower ribs. When he fell both barrels of his gun were found cocked. Woods died before morning. The verdict of the coriner's jury was justifyable homicide.

KILLED.—On Tuesday evening, the 16th inst., deputy sheriff E. A. McKinney went to Wilson's saw-mill, about twenty-four miles northwest of Opelousas, to arrest a celored man, by the name of Simon Woods, charged with horse stealing, and assault and battery. Upon his arrival there, Mr. Wilson warned him of the desperate character of the negro, who, he said, was armed with a double barrel shot gun, and had threatened to kill any man who would attempt to arrest him. McKinney changed clothes with one of the workmen at the mill, so that the accused might not recognize him and make his escape. The man who had changed clothes with McKinney rode off as though coming to town, while McKinney took his place at work at the mill to await the expected arrival of Woods. In the meantime he had secured a shot gun to protect himself, in case the negro should attempt to use his gun in resisting arrest. Late in the evening, Woods made his appearance armed with a shot gun and evidently expecting the arrival of an officer to arrest him. McKinney approached him, and asked if he was Simon Woods. He replied that he was. McKinney then said to him, "I have a warrant to arrest you, and you are my prisoner." Woods picked up his gun, when McKinney leveled his gun at the same time, and told him to drop his gun or he would shoot him. But instead of heeding the warning, Woods cocked both barrels of his gun and commenced raising it to his shoulder. McKinney fired just in time to save his own life, shooting Woods in the bowels, from which wound he died the next morning. Before dying, he stated that the officer had done right in shooting him; because he was determined not to be arrested, or go to jail again. Woods had been in this parish for two years, and was a fugitive from St. Martin parish, where he escaped from jail, under a charge of stabbing a man with intent to murder. He was said to be a dangerous and desperate character.

A Rare Villain.
Last Thursday, 9th instant, a white man who has been traveling through the County selling garden seed, was in No. 6 Township. He went to a gentleman's plantation and asked a negro on the place if the gentleman was at home. Being told that he was not, he said that he would not go to the house. But he did go. He knocked at the door, and the lady came to the door and opened it. The fellow there used the most insulting language to her. She slammed the door in his face; but he opened it and walked in. She fled into the kitchen in the back part of the house. He pursued her there, and she fled out of the house and into the house of a colored family near by. The fellow then left. When the husband came home at night and heard of the affair he was, of course, very angry; and, with some of his neighbors started out early Friday morning after the fellow. Had they caught him he would have fared badly. After riding about fifty miles they returned, and telegraphed to Laurens for the arrest of the fellow if found. He was arrested at Laurens and brought down on the train Saturday morning and placed in jail. He says he is from Buncombe County, North Carolina, and that his name is Spain.

Saturday there were threats of lynching, but wise counsels prevailed and everything became quiet. Monday evening it began to be whispered about that Spain would be taken from the jail. From what can be learned it was the intention to take him out, give him a decent threshing and turn him loose. The Sheriff getting wind of the matter called out a posse to guard the jail, and thus frustrated the plan. When everything had become quiet, and the crowd had dispersed, Trial Justice Fair, upon whose warrant Spain had been committed, sent an order of release to the Sheriff, and Spain was turned out. When released he did not tarry, but left at the top of his speed, and has not since been heard from.

A Young Wife Brutally Shot by a Hired Man.
Mrs. Joseph Copeland, of Hopedale, O., the Victim—The Murderer Confesses His Guilt—Threats of Lynching, But Better Counsel Prevails and He Will
BE PERMITTED TO PULL HEMP.
