HOPEDALE, O., August 31.—This staid and quiet little village was thrown into a fever of excitement by a telegram stating that a former resident of the vicinity had been murdered a few hours before.

The facts, as understood by your correspondent, are as follows: Mr. and Mrs. Joseph Copeland having linked their destinies, moved to Kewanee, Coles county, Illinois, for the purpose of locating, which they did some three or four years ago.

They visited friends here last winter, and upon their return were accompanied by a Mr. T. C. Bell, an old neighbor, and a young man by the name of Sylvester Machinson, he going for the purpose of finding employment, which he did a few days after their arrival.

A few days ago Mr. Copeland and Mr. Bell were called away on business, and upon their return found the body of Mrs. C. in the yard, mangled and bleeding, with two bullet holes in her breast and a severe cut on the forehead, supposed to have been made by a heavy instrument.

The object of the murderer was evidently to obtain money, eighty dollars belonging to Mr. Bell having been taken. Suspicion at once centered upon young Machinson as the guilty one, and he was arrested and the money and a revolver, with two empty chambers, were found upon his person.

The body of the victim was brought here yesterday and laid to rest in a neighboring cemetery, amid a host of sorrowing friends.

Further Particulars.

The Enquirer publishes the following additional facts in regard to the murder: At Kewanee, a farm hand who had been at work in that locality called at a farm house in the neighborhood. Here he found a lady alone, and after some delay he brutally murdered her by blows and by pistol shots, robbed the house of some money and departed, but some hours later joined in the search for the murderer, the body of the murdered lady having been found. He was subsequently arrested on suspicion, and finally on Monday confessed his crime. The discovery of this atrocity, together with the arrest and confession of the murderer, happening at the same time as the discovery and arrest of the bank robbers, naturally has given Kewanee an excitement that rarely falls to the lot of a rural town.

The examination of Makinson, the murderer of Mrs. Copeland, was held this forenoon. He waived examination and pleaded guilty, and was remanded to the county jail. Fully five thousand men were on the streets at an early hour this morning, determined that Makison should be hung before he left the place, but by the exertions of some of the, best citizens, coupled with the assurance of State's Attorney Gilchrist that the law should be fully carried out, he was allowed to be taken by the officers to the county jail.

An hour from the time he was removed it would have been impossible to have taken him from the court room without the citizens having taken him in charge and hanged him on the spot. Before taking him to the court room he made a full confession of the crime and gave all the particulars, telling where the stolen property was concealed, which was found as he described. No attempt to violate the person of Mrs. Copeland was made. He claims that he can give no explanation why he did the deed, as Mrs. Copeland was a good friend to him and had been very kind to him many times. Before being taken from the jail to the Court-room for examination he begged the officers to allow the crowd to hang him immediately, he wishing to die as soon as possible. Makison's confession was secured by a Pinkerton detective who was locked up in the same cell with him, and who made Makison believe he was Welch, the bank robber. A mutual interchange of confidence led to a full disclosure by the murder of all the details of his awful crime. Makison was taken to Cambridge Jail this afternoon, some twenty miles away, and there confined. He was willing to be handed over to the mob, saying that he knew he should be hung anyhow, and wanted to have it over at once.

The Leesburg Washingtonian gives the sequel as follows:

"On Thursday, the Sheriff learned of the organization of a party, in the neighborhood where the crime was committed, to take the prisoner from the jail on Thursday night and lynch him. He took the necessary precaution to prevent it. Pickets were placed on the roads approaching the town, and about 12 o'clock at night they brought information that a large body of horsemen were coming down the Leesburg turnpike. Upon learning this, the Sheriff went to the Court House and rung the bell, to arouse the citizens to assist him, if necessary, in maintaining the law, but before he could get back to the jail the first squad of raiders, about twenty in number, came thundering down Market Street, from the direction of the Fair Ground, in cavalry style, and brought up in front of the jail—some with their faces covered, others with nothing but the shades of night to prevent them from being discovered. They were met at the jail by the Jailor and his sons; the Sheriff soon returned from the Court House; no citizens had yet arrived. The raiders' judgment seemed to fail them at the critical moment—they sat quietly for a moment or two on their horses—not a man dismounted—not a word was spoken—they took in the surroundings, and not knowing what to do, wisely concluded to turn round and dashed out Market Street, as they came in. In a few moments another squad approached the jail from the East, up the Alexandria pike, and, without halting, rode on out of town. By this time a number of our citizens had assembled. No further disturbance occurred. No attempt was made to enter the jail. It was more a midnight frolic than a serious attempt at lynching. Those who had the best opportunity of judging think there were about forty or fifty in the party. The only thing that the raiders did, that looked like business, in the farce they played at lynching, was the annoyance they gave one of our citizens, in holding him a prisoner in the charge of a guard in the road near the Fair Ground, until they had marched down to town and marched back again."

"All the mountain lands in Craig county have been purchased within the last two years. They are finely timbered and full of ore. Much of the land, which but a short time ago was considered worthless, cannot be purchased now scarcely at any price."

The above is a very small paragraph, found in one of our exchanges, and like many of its kind is read without considering for a moment all the meaning it contains. This is a sample of the many transactions of the kind that are daily occurring and which swell into business proportions, and dot the history of the county or State in which they take place with what is called "progress." The term is not inaptly used, but who are the beneficiaries of this progress. Certainly not the people of Craig county, who have sold their timber and ore lands at from $3 to $5 per acre, as the case may be, and have since awakened to the fact that the capitalists who became the purchasers thereof are the possessors of property worth from $20 to $30 per acre—perhaps more. If the people, or original owners of the lands sold, had reaped a liberal share of the benefits to accrue to the monopolists that have become their purchasers, one might feel disposed to rejoice in this sort of progress. Virginia contains a vast amount of undeveloped riches, but until Virginians learn how to use their capital for the development of these stores of wealth, they must expect to see the profits flow into the pockets of the new invaders from the North.

A Vile Murderer Kills Himself.
CLEVELAND, April 25.—A Herald special from Canton states that about sunrise this morning William Stull, the Georgetown murderer, was cornered in some dense woods near New Franklin, fourteen miles southeast of Canton, by the Columbiana county sheriff and a posse of deputies, who had been following him since Sunday. Finding escape impossible he drew his revolver, with which he murdered Mrs. Sommers, and fired two shots into his head in quick succession, producing instant death. The excitement is intense in Stark and Columbiana counties.

The particulars of the vile wretch's most cowardly and revolting crime are as follows: Collins Summers, one of the most prominent farmers of Columbiana county, has had a hired hand named Wm. Stull in his employ for the past year or two; about ten days ago he discharged him on account of his quarrelsome disposition and since that time Stull has been lurking in the neighborhood. Late on Sunday Mrs. Summers was at the barn, milking her cow, when she saw Stull approaching, little dreaming of his murderous intent or of the horrible fate which awaited her. He came and stood within a few feet of Mrs. Sommers and said "Good evening." She noticed nothing wrong in his behavior, and, after answering him very pleasantly, resumed her work. Scarcely had she turned her back, when her cowardly assin deliberately drew his six shooter revolver and emptied the contents of all the chambers in the body of his innocent and defenceless victim, two of the balls taking a fatal effect, one in her breast and the other through her spine. The inhuman monster then fled, and the family were horified, on rushing to the barn, to behold the victim of the wretch weltering in her own gore. Stull accused Mrs. Summers as being instrumental in having him discharged, and this was the trivial pretext for his murdering her in cold blood.

Murder and Suicide.
Last Sunday morning, William Stull, a farm-hand who had been working for Collins Summers, near North Georgetown, Columbiana county, but discharged a few weeks previously, went to the barn where Mrs. Summers was milking, and after bidding her good morning, drew a revolver and fired five shots at her, one striking her in the back, hitting the spinal column, causing paralysis of the lower part of the body; a second took effect back of the left armpit, running around to the breast bone. The third struck her just above the knee. The murderer fled and was tracked to the neighborhood of Osnaburg by the officers, and on Tuesday morning the Sheriff of Columbiana county and six deputies caught sight of him in the woods near New Franklin, and surrounded him. Finding escape impossible, he drew the same revolver that did the shooting, placed it to his forehead, pulled the trigger and fell, dying in a few moments. He was barely 23 years old, and bore a grudge against Mrs. Summers, as he thought she had secured his discharge from the farm. Mrs. Summers is lying in a critical condition.
